Ratnamani just won a big order for spooling business.

What differentiates spooling vs normal piping business?

-Plain pipe is a spread business on a pass-through. Price per tonne is roughly steel cost plus a conversion charge. Steel is 65–75% of the selling price and moves with HRC/plate/billet indices, so the mill's real economics are a thin conversion spread sitting on top of a large pass-through base. 

-Two consequences: (a) the margin percentage is arithmetically compressed because the denominator is inflated by material the mill never really "owned" economically, and (b) the product is fungible — once two mills are on the same approved vendor list for API 5L X65, the buyer runs a reverse auction and price converges to the marginal supplier's cost plus a sliver.

Spooling sells something else entirely: avoided site work. 

-A spool is pipe cut to isometric drawings, welded to elbows, tees, reducers and flanges, radiographed, hydro-tested, PWHT'd where needed, coated, tagged, and shipped as a numbered assembly that gets bolted or tied in at site. What the customer is buying is the elimination of field welds.

-That's where the margin comes from, and it's the key first principle: your margin is set by the gap between your cost to do the work and the customer's cost to do it themselves. Shop welding with positioners, jigs and automated processes runs several times more productive per joint than field welding.

-Do that same weld on an offshore platform or inside a live refinery during a turnaround, and you're paying for scaffolding, access, hot-work permits, weather windows, vessel or barge day-rates, and the big one is deferred production for every day the shutdown runs long. The client's alternative cost is enormous, so willingness-to-pay is anchored to their avoided cost, not to your input cost. Pricing shifts from cost-plus to value-based.

Thus, in recent quarterly result. Ratnamani generated nearly 52% EBITDA MARGINS from the spooling division.

Just read the following Para carefully from Nephrocare's concall and understand why Dialysis is a difficult business to be profitable at.

Dialysis looks like a wonderful business on paper i.e. recurring revenue, non-discretionary demand, a patient who comes back three times a week for years. NephroPlus is the cleanest Indian case study for why it isn't, and the numbers are unusually honest about it.

1. You don't set the price. The payer does.

This is the root problem. Dialysis pricing in India runs around $22–25 per session, while the Philippines operates at roughly $110 per treatment for the identical clinical procedure, same machine, same consumables, 4–5x the realisation. That gap has nothing to do with cost or quality; it reflects what the payer can afford. In India the payer is largely the government (PPP tenders), insurance schemes, or a price-sensitive self-payer. You bid for volume in a tender; you don't price to value.

Watch how NephroPlus actually improved its realisation: blended RPT rose 13.3% in FY26 to ₹2,598, and 9.2% in Q1FY27 to ₹2,733. But that's mix, not pricing power as international went from 12% of revenue in FY23 to ~41% in 9MFY26 and 45% by Q1FY27. The company fixed its unit economics by leaving India, not by winning in it.

2. Cost per session is fixed, imported, and non-negotiable.

Dialyzer, tubing, dialysate, needles, EPO, plus nurse and technician time, every session consumes roughly the same basket. Machines and RO plants are largely imported. So you have a capped price and a floor on variable cost. Gross margin per session is structurally thin, and the only lever left is utilisation.

3. Utilisation is the whole game, but geography fights you.

Management says it plainly: dialysis is fundamentally a scale-driven business where higher volume drives operating leverage, asset utilisation and ROCE. But dialysis is a four-hour treatment required multiple times a week, which makes proximity critical as over 75% of NephroPlus's Indian clinics sit in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Patients won't travel, so you must build small clinics close to them. Small clinics mean few machines, and a machine either runs its three shifts or it doesn't. Breakeven is a step function, not a curve. A greenfield clinic takes about 12 months to reach operational breakeven versus 3–4 months for an acquired one — so every year of expansion carries a drag cohort.

4. The financial history is the evidence.

Founded 2009–10. Raised roughly $205M across 13 rounds from 33 investors. For first 11 years of its life, Nephro was EBITDA negative and for 13 years it was PAT negative. High fixed cost businesses need massive scale to generate margins.

One of the easiest mistakes in investing is annualising a great quarter.

Valiant Laboratories just reported ~25% operating margins in Q1 FY27.

The stock quickly moved from roughly Rs. 60 to Rs. 95.

And there are genuine reasons for the improvement.

Valiant has backward integrated into Acetic Anhydride, one of the key raw materials used in manufacturing Paracetamol API.

Another important raw material, PAP, is largely imported into India from China. Valiant, however, sources it from its group Company, Valiant Organics.

So the improvement in economics is real.

But here is the problem.

Paracetamol API is not structurally a 25%+ margin business.

It is closer to a 10–15% margin business under normal economics.

Which means the mistake would be to take this quarter's profitability and assume this is the new base.

If margins normalise from 25% towards historical industry economics, earnings can look very different from what annualising Q1 suggests.

And Valiant is probably not the only example.

Q1 FY27 has thrown up some spectacular results across Companies. But a great quarter does not necessarily mean the earnings trajectory has permanently changed.

The real question is not how good the quarter was.

It is how much of that quarter is sustainable.

That distinction becomes especially important when the stock price has already started extrapolating the good news.

MODISONS

The tiny component sitting inside India’s electrification story

Most people have never heard of Modison. But its products sit inside the equipment that controls some of the most critical electricity infrastructure.

Modison manufactures electrical contacts and contact materials used in circuit breakers, contactors and switchgear across low, medium, high and extra-high voltage applications. Its portfolio includes silver-alloy contacts, copper-tungsten contacts, crowns, brazing assemblies, bimetal rivets, cladded contacts and specialised alloys. In simple words, Modison makes the tiny metal parts that connect and disconnect electricity safely.

And this is where the story gets interesting.

In high-voltage contacts, Modison estimates it has ~80–82% market share in India and says it is the only Indian manufacturer of specialised “crowns”. These components are designed into breakers supplied to customers such as GE, ABB, Siemens, BHEL and BEL. Replacing a qualified contact supplier is not like changing a normal vendor — the component has to be tested and qualified for the specific breaker design, creating years of switching friction.

The ISRO example shows how difficult this capability can be to replicate. ISRO had reportedly tried 5–6 suppliers over 5–6 years for a Russian-standard brazing alloy foil. Modison developed the import substitute in just 8–10 months and became the qualified domestic supplier. That is much more interesting than simply saying “Modison has good technology.”

There is another important advantage: Modison is vertically integrated. It can refine silver, manufacture contact materials and then manufacture the finished contacts itself. It also has an in-house tool room, R&D capability and testing infrastructure. Around 260 new customer-specific products were developed in FY26 — these are not simple catalogue products, but parts designed around customer specifications.

Now comes the growth opportunity.

India is entering a long power-infrastructure cycle. More renewable generation means more transmission infrastructure. More factories, metros, EV infrastructure and data centres mean more switchgear. Management specifically highlighted data centres and AI as a demand driver because more data-centre power infrastructure requires more switchgear and therefore more electrical contacts.

The pipeline is broader than just India. Modison wants exports to cross ₹100 crore in FY27 and has identified 20–25 large international prospects. It is also working on high-voltage products, silver-thrifting solutions, specialised alloys and tungsten recovery. The company has set revenue targets of ₹880 crore for FY27 and ₹1,365 crore by FY30.

But investors need to understand one very important catch.

Modison is not yet a pure high-margin specialty company.

Around 80% of sales come from low/medium-voltage products, where management estimates only ~30–35% Indian market share and where silver accounts for 75–80% of raw-material cost. FY26 revenue jumped 45% to ₹716 crore and EBITDA rose 143% to ₹115 crore, but a large part of the reported growth was helped by the huge increase in silver prices.

This is why I would not simply extrapolate FY26 margins.

The real test for Modison is whether it can gradually shift the mix from “silver conversion” to “mission-critical engineering.”

If high-voltage contacts, crowns, specialised alloys, exports, data-centre demand and grid infrastructure become a much larger part of the business, the quality of earnings could improve materially.

If not, Modison could remain a cyclical silver-processing business with a very attractive niche attached to it.

That is the real investment question.

The moat is real. The opportunity is real. But the next few years will tell us whether Modison can turn a small high-voltage toll bridge into the main highway.

Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

First CAS Manipulation found.

SEBI has passed an ex-parte interim order against an FPI and a local stockbroker, for what it calls prima facie manipulation of CAS on 13 August and wrongful gains of ₹3.67 crore.

What really happened?

It was Sensex weekly expiry. Inside the auction window the index moved 362 points in two seconds, then 405 points in 28 seconds.

1. Copthall Mauritius was 86.6% of the entire gross buy value in that auction. Every order across all 30 Sensex stocks at exactly 3% above reference price, the maximum the band allows. Then it cancelled ₹98 crore of them once the move had happened. 

It held long calls and short puts on that expiry. Spent ₹57 lakh in the cash market, made ₹2.96 crore in derivatives.

2. Mansi Share and Stock Broking did the reverse. 

₹145 crore of sell orders below reference price, holding the index down while it exited its long puts, then cancelled 99% of them in three seconds. 

That cancellation alone moved the Sensex 233 points.

JUBILANT INGREVIA: From Pyridine to PCBs

A chemicals company with 45+ years of legacy in pyridine and acetic anhydride just paid ₹189.2 crore for 40% of an electronics design firm. Sounds like random diversification. It isn't.

Jubilant Ingrevia already sells into the semiconductor value chain, just one layer down. Its CDMO arm makes ultra-high-purity chemicals for chip and display manufacturing: E-Pyridine, E-Choline, photoresist precursors, display intermediates. The fab customer relationships already exist.

What Jubilant structurally cannot build in-house is what Zettaone brings. Co-founded about two decades ago, it does R&D, design, prototyping, manufacturing, assembly and box build for aerospace, defence, semiconductor, automotive, medical and industrial customers. The pitch to those shared customers becomes: we don't just supply your chemicals, we can design and build your electronics too.

Zettaone's turnover: ₹51.1cr in FY24, ₹79.1cr in FY25, ₹98.1cr in FY26. Growth decelerating from +55% to +24%.

₹189.2cr for 40% implies roughly ₹473cr for the whole company, about 4.8x sales.

40% makes Zettaone an associate, not a subsidiary. It won't consolidate. Jubilant gets an equity-accounted share of profit and no control over the business it's backing.

A genuinely interesting angle on India's electronics localisation push, entered through a side door nobody was watching.
